item.title: Are You Controlling? Anxiety May Be to Blame
item.description:
Anxiety

Are You Controlling? Anxiety May Be to Blame

If you want to be in control all the time, you are probably trying to feel safe.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • If you feel anxious, it's natural to seek control in all areas of your life.
  • But much of life is beyond our control, such as the aging process.
  • This means that seeking control often makes us more anxious, not less.
Source: Alexandra Gorn/Unsplash

Nobody likes feeling out of control, unless we are enjoying the safe-but-scary thrills of a rollercoaster or horror movie. When it comes to the important stuff of life, like our intimate relationships, health, and finances, we all like to feel in control.

But if you struggle with anxiety, you are likely to be especially sensitive to feeling out of control. You may also seek certainty, trying to think ahead and plan for every eventuality.

Anxious Inner Child

As I explain in my new book, Heal Your Trauma: How to Overcome a Painful Childhood to Become Happy and Whole Again, viewed through a schema therapy or internal family systems (IFS) lens, this means you have an anxious inner child, feeling small, scared, and vulnerable. A cluster of protective parts around this anxious little one are working hard to keep them safe. These protectors might include a perfectionist, who makes sure you never make mistakes so you can never be criticised, blamed, or attacked if things go wrong.

You will probably have an inner worrier, worrying away 24/7 when that little part feels anxious, doing all the mental bridge-crossing that helps you anticipate threats or dangers up ahead and try to problem-solve them. There will likely also be an avoider, helping you avoid the things that make you anxious, such as parties or public speaking.

The (Reassuring) Illusion of Control

You will probably have a controller, the protective part we are focusing on here. This part seeks control at all times and in every area of your life. But it may show up more in some areas than others, perhaps helping you control your children so they never risk being hurt or falling behind at school. For others, work is their hot-button issue, so they try to be (or at least appear) in control all the time, maintaining a polished, professional appearance, even if they are panicking inside.

The problem is, although we may seek control in many areas of our lives, it can be impossible most of the time. Humans do not exist in a vacuum. We live in systems, both large and small. Our first system is our family, born or later chosen. Next comes our friends and colleagues, our community, city or town, country, and ultimately the entire human system of eight billion fellow souls, with whom we are inextricably linked in many ways.

As any parent knows, it’s hard enough to control your children (parenting toddlers or teenagers, anyone?), let alone any of the other people in your orbit. Here’s a short list of things we might like to control, but sadly have little or no power over:

  • Aging and mortality, of those we love and ourselves
  • Hormonal cycles, especially for women, both monthly and over a lifetime (like perimenopause)
  • The economy
  • The weather
  • Climate change
  • Political systems, local and national
  • What others think of us
  • The behaviour of those we love and rely on

Relinquishing Control

*Katherine came to see me because she had just been diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, a common diagnosis for people with chronic worry and anxiety. She worried incessantly, often lying awake until 3 am worrying about her kids, health issues, and political causes she was passionate about, such as climate change and the potentially harmful impact of AI. "Worry just makes me crazy," she told me. "I know it’s not rational, but I can’t help myself; the thoughts just swirl round and round in my head until sleep is impossible."

Poor Katherine was exhausted, getting five hours’ sleep on a good night and just two or three on bad ones. But struggling with insomnia like this is common for anxiety gripping their belly and worry spinning round and round in their heads. To help Katherine, we first identified the cluster of protective parts trying to keep Little Katherine safe. All of the above protectors were present in her inner system, but her dominant protector was the controller. "My kids get so mad with me because I micromanage them all the time," she admitted. "My husband too. They call me a control freak, and they're not wrong."

When we gave this part a voice, we learned it meant no harm, quite the opposite. Katherine grew up with two alcoholic parents, in a home full of drunken chaos, screaming and fighting. As a child, she learned to control what she could—keeping her clothes clean, lining up her dolls in neat rows, making sure her schoolwork was always perfect. These healthy, adaptive coping responses to the chaos of her childhood got wired into her brain, because she repeated them over and over for years, until they formed the protective parts that now drove her family crazy and kept her up half the night.

Helping Protectors Relax

Using the IFS "healing steps," we got permission to help Little Katharine and processed the traumatic memories that made her so anxious. When she felt calmer and safer, we could then help the protectors relax and take a well-earned break. We also set her concrete, behavioural homework that involves letting her kids live freer, healthily riskier lives (climbing trees, riding their bikes, having sleepovers with friends). Little by little, as her controller relaxed, so could Katherine.

This brought calm and ease to her family, which also made Katherine happy. "It's weird, because I always thought I needed to be in control all the time to keep everyone safe," she said in our last session, "but I now realise I was holding on way too tight. The more I relax, the more my family does too. I had to let go!"

If this resonates with you, get to know your inner system, especially protectors busting a gut to keep you safe. You might need some help from a skilled, parts-based therapist to untangle the tight ball of protection in your mind. But remember that the secret to a life with greater contentment, ease, and joy lies in learning to let go, a little.

The protection you needed as a little kid is probably too much for your adult self. Life is too short to waste with well-meaning, but ultimately self-defeating attempts at constant control.

*All case studies in these posts are composites; I never tell the stories of real clients, as confidentiality is very important to me.

item.title: Why Does Yoga Feel Like Coming Home?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Does Yoga Feel Like Coming Home?

What yoga can teach us about listening to ourselves.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Yoga gives us the space to listen to what our bodies are trying to tell us.
  • A yoga practice can help us meet stress with more awareness and self-compassion.
  • Sometimes yoga is less about what your body can do and more about what it needs.
Source: Jared Rice/Unsplash

When I was 16, I first walked into a yoga studio. The lighting was dim, the music was zen, and the décor oozed comfort and calm. My nervous system seemed to let out a big sigh, and my whole body immediately felt more grounded. It felt like I had arrived home.

Unfortunately, it didn’t last. When I tried to sign up, I was told they didn’t allow students under 18. I was heartbroken, but I walked out knowing that I would find my way back to yoga one day.

It took another decade before I fully embraced it. Within that decade, I dabbled. I tried a gym yoga class that was far too fitness-oriented; a beach holiday class where the teacher clearly didn’t want to be there; and a trendy London class where I felt like most people were there simply because yoga was cool.

I was looking for something else. I wanted yoga that connected me to myself and my well-being. I wanted something that went beyond fitness and into the mind, body, and spirit connection.

So, in the middle of a difficult breakup, I started following yoga videos on YouTube. I started, and I never really stopped. I quickly found Yoga with Adriene, whose guidance I’ve followed ever since. I’ve tried other classes and even a week-long retreat, but it's practicing at home that I love most. Partly because my dog Bond likes to join me, adding challenges such as sitting his 34-kilogram body on me during an ab workout or licking my face when I'm in downward dog.

Mostly, though, I love being able to adapt my practice to whatever I need. Tired? I can choose a relaxing yin practice. Full of energy? I can do something more dynamic. Only have 15 minutes? There’s a quick flow for that. That's the beauty of yoga. Over the years, it has taught me to listen to my body and give it what it needs.

All of this made me wonder: why does yoga make me feel so good?

So I dived into the research and discovered that some of what I’ve experienced is beginning to show up in the science, too.

1. Yoga brings you back into your body.

One of the things I love most about yoga is that it asks me to pay attention to what is happening inside me. How does this stretch feel? Am I holding my breath? Do I need to soften? Is my body telling me that's enough?

This awareness of our internal bodily sensations is called interoception. A 2025 systematic review of yoga interventions found promising evidence that yoga can improve body awareness. This makes total sense to me. Yoga gives me a reason to stop thinking about everything else and simply notice what is happening here, in this body, right now.

2. Yoga can make your body feel more spacious.

Yoga obviously involves stretching, but I think there is something more subtle happening than simply becoming more flexible. With regular practice, the shoulders soften, the spine moves more freely, and you become more comfortable inhabiting your body, not just on the mat but also off the mat.

Research supports this idea. Another systematic review from 2024 found that yoga can improve spinal and shoulder mobility, although the effects varied according to the individual and the type of yoga practised. I love that yoga doesn’t ask my body to become something it isn’t. It simply gives it more space to move.

3. Yoga can help soften stress.

There is a reason I often feel calmer after yoga than I did before I started. There is a reason my dog falls asleep next to me when I'm in corpse pose. Yoga brings together movement, breathing, and attention, giving the mind fewer places to run off to. Instead of replaying yesterday or worrying about tomorrow, I concentrate on the stretch I’m in, the breath I’m taking, and the body I’m inhabiting.

Studies have started to show that yoga can reduce stress and may also help with symptoms of anxiety. It might not be a magic cure, but it can help us meet stress and anxiety differently. This is one of the biggest lessons I've learned from yoga: not judging where I'm at, but meeting myself there and seeing how I can support myself.

4. Yoga can offer you a different relationship with yourself.

Yoga has taught me that I don’t have to push my body every day. Sometimes I need strength. Sometimes I need movement. Sometimes I need stillness. That is a surprisingly powerful lesson to take off the yoga mat.

A 2026 study of stressed adults taking part in a 12-week yoga programme found increases in self-compassion and interoceptive awareness, which were further associated with greater feelings of peace and meaning in life. Perhaps this is why yoga can feel so different from traditional forms of exercise. It isn’t asking, “What can my body do?” It's asking, “What does my body need?” And there is a world of difference between the two.

This is why I see yoga as much more than movement. It's a practice, a mindset, and, for me, a way of being. It has taught me to slow down enough to listen, to notice without immediately judging, and to meet myself where I am rather than constantly pushing towards where I think I should be. Maybe that is why, all those years ago, I walked into a yoga studio at 16 and felt something in me exhale. A part of me already knew what I was looking for. I was looking for a practice to bring me home to myself.

May you be healthy. May you be happy. May you be at peace, wherever you are.

item.title: Stop Being Your Partner's Parent
item.description:
Relationships

Stop Being Your Partner's Parent

If you want mature intimacy, let go of the monopoly.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • In the parent/child dynamic, one partner over-functions and the other under-functions.
  • The parent-partner gains control and may become bitter and rigid.
  • The child-partner gains freedom, but is not respected. This hierarchy hurts the sexual and intimate bonds.
Source: Kibbutz Keturah

Co-authored with Galit Romanelli

"He didn't understand your question."

I had just asked Eli a question, and as he was pondering his answer, Dana jumped in. "He thinks it's because I'm too strict with the kids. He doesn't understand that it's because he's not present." This was the third time she answered for him.

"Thank you," I said, "but let me talk to him directly. He's a big boy and he'll ask me to clarify if he doesn't understand."

"But I'm seeing you miscommunicate."

"It's happening right now. I'm having a moment with Eli, and you're getting activated as if he's a child who doesn't understand my question. Let me and him sort it out. Every time you come to 'help him,' you're locking you two as mommy and child."

They nodded.

They came because Dana was tired of singlehandedly managing their marriage and home. With two small kids under 6, they were in the classic parent/child dynamic I often see in the clinic.

How Two Adults Become Parent and Child

A few weeks earlier, Dana had asked me: "How can I stop being the always-right, reliable mother, if he continues to not show up... Who's going to file our taxes? Who will pay the bills? Too many times Eli didn't do his part. So no, from now on, he can't mess up anymore, because I took everything over."

The parent/child dynamic in heterosexual couples often looks the same. The wife is what I call a "married single mother." She runs the kids. She cooks, helps with homework, knows what's going on, and holds it all, all the time. Across from her is "the third child" or "the babysitter," who drops by now and then and yells at her from the bleachers: "Hey, you're not doing that right."

In couples therapy, we call this over-functioning and under-functioning. It also happens the other way around. Previously we described this hierarchy in parenting as the upstairs and downstairs parent. Now we focus on what it does to the marriage.

Why We Do It

Often this is a result of intergenerational replication, models we saw as children. I asked Dana how her mom would complete the sentence "Men are..." She didn't miss a beat: "Men are little children. She never really respected my father." They both chuckled.

"That's a core belief," I said. "You’re a loyal daughter who’s replicating that script. You're proving your mom right."

Dana, like all of us, saw Eli through the lens of the core beliefs she inherited, which usually led to a self-fulfilling prophecy. Add classic gender roles, and you end up with the stigma of the "overbearing mother" and the "irresponsible man-boy."

What the Parent-Partner Gets

It was time to list Dana's secondary gains and losses for being her husband's mom. She easily named her losses. "Everything rests on my shoulders. I feel lonely and alone, and I long for a real meaningful partnership."

Then we listed her secondary gains. "I'm independent. I'm in charge and I'm in control." We brainstormed more benefits: protection from being vulnerable, monopoly over the child-rearing and family life, being always right, and Eli being an easy excuse for why she's not living her best life. Thanks to Eli under-functioning as the third child, she's the queen of the castle.

A partner who parents their spouse ultimately becomes heavy, bitter, and rigid. They become the bad cop who's not fun to be around. They become a know-it-all. It's not sexy. And their child-partner starts to avoid them.

What the Child-Partner Gets

Why would anyone agree to be seen as the third child? Freedom. No responsibility. "I have loads of time, I can focus on myself, I'm flexible."

The biggest loss is their partner's respect. The third child isn't sexy and isn't appreciated. At some point, their voice isn't heard. Even when they're right, they get disqualified, because "you don't really know what you're talking about."

The price both partners pay is a relationship with little mature sexuality, no deep intimacy, and no equitable partnership. Kids who live in this hierarchy usually replicate a similar relationship.

How to Soften It

  • Own your role. Use the Integrity Chart to review your losses and gains to prepare for the costs of such change.

  • Give it a code word. Code words help add play and soften the hierarchy. Dana and Eli chose "Mars" for when she is locked in seeing him as immature, and "Snickers" for when he can only see her as the disappointed mother.

  • Lead with your wise adult. When you recognize you're engaging from the parent or child, reengage from the relational partner, the wise and balanced part of you.

If you're the child

Take responsibility. Say "I got this." Fewer words, more action. Hold on to your truth: say "In my experience…" and stand up behind what you believe. Be ready to take flack for it. Remember that next to every bitter mother-partner there's a man who, in some way, isn't taking enough responsibility.

If you're the parent

Let go of control. Don't micromanage. Ask your partner to take more responsibility. Accept that they won't do it your way, and mourn the change while lowering your standards. Allow yourself to lean.

The biggest shift is to accept their narrative of reality. You want to enter a two-narrative relationship. You're doing this because you want a partner and you don't want to be alone. If you want a partner, you're going to have to let go of the monopoly of your one-narrative relationship.

Both of you

Adopt a playful mindset. Be soft and forgiving. Know that this change will reshape your whole relationship. And it won't be smooth.

If Dana and Eli want to remarry each other, they will have to dare to meet as equals. To meet in the truth. Only then will they truly feel free together.

Don't be your partner's parent. Be your partner's partner.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.
